title: Lag BaOmer
hookLine: the thirty-third day breaks the mourning with bonfires, linked to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai

cards: For weeks, the season has been quiet. In many communities, there have been no weddings, no live music, no haircuts, and people look a little shaggy.
Then, on one night in late spring, all over Israel, the sky fills with smoke. Kids have collected scrap wood for days: pallets, old doors, fruit crates.
Bonfires burn in parks and empty lots, and families roast potatoes in the coals. In the north, huge crowds pour into a small town to sing and dance around a tomb.
The next morning, the barbers are busy and the wedding halls are full.

teach.b: Lag BaOmer means the thirty-third of the Omer. Hebrew letters are also numbers: lamed is thirty, gimel is three, and together they're said lag. On this day the Omer's mourning customs, which come tomorrow, are lifted.
Honestly, the reasons came after the custom. A tradition from the Middle Ages says a plague among Rabbi Akiva's students stopped that day.
A later tradition, from the mystics of Safed, says it's the anniversary of the death of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, one of Akiva's students. The Talmud tells his story.
He criticized the Roman rulers, was sentenced to death, and hid with his son in a cave for twelve years.
A carob tree and a spring appeared to keep them alive, and they studied all day, buried in sand up to their necks to save their clothes.

Tradition credits him with the Zohar, a foundational book of Kabbalah; modern historians argue it was written much later, in medieval Spain, and traditional readers keep the older attribution. Both views are held today.
The mystics taught that on the day he died, he revealed his deepest secrets and the house filled with light.

teach.h: A DEATH DAY TURNED TO LIGHT.
teach.b: So a death day became a hilula, the wedding-feast of a soul, and the bonfires are said to recall his light. His tomb is in Meron, in the Galilee, which is why the crowds go there.
In some communities, children get their first haircut there, and play with bows and arrows.
After weeks of quiet, a break in the sadness.

how: On Lag BaOmer, the thirty-third day of the Omer, the season's mourning customs are lifted: weddings and haircuts resume, bonfires are lit, especially in Israel, and crowds make pilgrimage to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's tomb in Meron.

games.q: you're Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, sentenced to death by Rome. what do you do?
o: hide in a cave with your son and study.
games.why: he hid in a cave with his son for twelve years, fed by a carob tree and a spring, studying all day.

practice: If you can, light a candle, safely, or sit by a fireplace, or just watch a flame on a screen.
Think of a long stretch that's been heavy for you or someone close, and let this one minute be a break in it: warmth, light, nothing to fix.
